title: THE GREAT CHINA RECKONING: Why Chinese AI models are cheaper, closer and better than you realise
description: Send us Fan Mail Frontier AI headlines make it sound like everything comes down to one scoreboard: China versus the US, best model versus second best. We don’t buy that framing. Living in China, we see a different story taking shape, where constraints on Nvidia GPUs, chip supply, and data centre power push Chinese labs and big tech firms towards efficiency and scale, not just bragging rights. A likely future sees US frontier models staying a few months ahead, Chinese models winning on real life use cases, affordability and efficiency. We start with the hard foundations: AI chips, export controls, and why Huawei Ascend matters even if it trails the cutting edge. From there we zoom out to infrastructure and energy, including China’s planned approach to building data centres where the power is, and what that changes when the West hits electricity and grid bottlenecks. We also touch on governance signals: cybersecurity law updates, AI ethics, safety frameworks, and the push to shape international AI standards. Then we get practical. We break down the Chinese AI model ecosystem people keep hearing about but rarely understand: DeepSeek, Qwen, Doubao, Tencent Yuanbao, Minimax, Kimi and GLM. We talk open source and open weights, why Hugging Face derivative models explode in number, and how quantisation makes powerful models usable on smaller hardware. Most importantly, we follow the money: token pricing, why “free” AI is being subsidised, and why cheap, capable models may end up running the background tasks that actually make businesses work. If you’re curious about Chinese AI models, open source LLMs, AI cost and compute, and where robotics and embodied AI fit next, listen through and tell us: which model would you trust for your day-to-day work? Subscribe, share, and leave a review if it helps.
summary: Living in China, Matt and Jimmy argue the frontier-scoreboard framing misses the real story: US export controls on chips pushed Chinese labs toward efficiency, open weights and brutal affordability rather than benchmark vanity. They tour the foundations — Huawei's Ascend 910C trailing TSMC by five to ten years but ramping to 1.6M dies, China's planned data-centre buildout 'where the power is' versus Western grid bottlenecks, and a 15-5-year plan targeting a 10-trillion-yuan AI industry by 2030 — then profile the actual ecosystem: DeepSeek, Qwen (100M active users, the volume leader), Doubao (which Matt's family 'Google' with), Tencent's WeChat-integrated Yuanbao, self-training MiniMax, Kimi, and GLM. The through-line is economics: Chinese models are 15–30% cheaper, dominate OpenRouter and Hugging Face (a hundred thousand derivative models), and are built to be routed invisibly into apps rather than admired. They close on the subsidy reckoning: 'free' AI was never free, and the cheap-model advantage is about to matter enormously.
keyTalkingPoints: Export controls backfired into a strategy: denied top Nvidia GPUs, Chinese labs optimized for efficiency, quantization and open weights — becoming 15–30% cheaper than international equivalents and 'good enough' for the tasks that actually pay.

Huawei's Ascend 910C acknowledges a five-to-ten-year lag on TSMC's 4nm process but could hit 1.6 million dies this year; China's real leverage is rare earth minerals, which is why Trump and Jensen Huang were both in Beijing this week.

China builds data centres where the power is, as a planned certainty ('the plan is this is what is going to happen'), while the West hits electricity and grid bottlenecks; AI-related industries are targeted at 10 trillion yuan (~$1.4T) by 2030.

The ecosystem is differentiated by ecosystem: Qwen owns Alibaba's e-commerce rails, Doubao is a verb for a hundred million users, Tencent's model has WeChat data access, Kimi ships agent-swarm research tooling — versus the US 'big four' all chasing the same AGI prize.

Chinese censorship is real but narrower than assumed (political topics, mostly in Chinese), and open weights let anyone unlock or quantize models — hence 100,000 Hugging Face derivatives and Chinese models permanently topping OpenRouter.

The free ride is ending: ~95% of users pay nothing while a maxed-out $20 Claude subscription costs Anthropic ~$180 in compute — Jimmy calls AI a bubble that pops within six months to two years, after which cheap Chinese models become the affordable backbone.

jimmy: He rejects the 'who's winning' scoreboard: China started second and focused on different areas — affordability and real-world use — and that focus is a direct result of US chip restrictions, not a grand design.
AI is a bubble that will pop within six months to two years; the free data-gathering era ends and AI gets much more expensive, which is exactly when cheap Chinese models become the sensible default.
He uses different AIs for different jobs and is pragmatic about Chinese models for casual use — while refusing to upload sensitive data to any model, US or Chinese.
He doesn't think ordinary people in the West need DeepSeek for recipes and letters yet — frontier subscriptions still cover that — but the cost crunch will change the calculus.
matt: China's plan-based model means its targets are effectively facts: 'if they say they're gonna do this, they'll just do whatever it takes to do it', and you can read the five-year plan to see 2030.

Chinese AI regulation is more substantive than the West assumes: the amended cybersecurity law covers AI algorithms, infrastructure and ethics, plus a lifecycle AI safety framework and a push to write 20 international AI standards.
He is careful not to be a 'CCP shill' — he presents the positive data alongside censorship and surveillance realities, and applies the same data-hygiene rules to US and Chinese models alike.

The economic use case for Chinese models is background work: chatbots, business automation and eventually robots — 'the robots will be coming from China, not from the US' because they're built for economic value, not brilliance.
